title: Galaxy LEDA 1313424 (Advanced Camera for Surveys Image)
caption: The Bullseye galaxy LEDA 1313424, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: LEDA 1313424 · constellation Pisces · about 567 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, Imad Pasha (Yale), Pieter van Dokkum (Yale)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A large galaxy sits at the centre with a much smaller one just to its left, against black space dotted with distant galaxies and a few foreground stars. The big one is LEDA 1313424, nicknamed the Bullseye, a collisional ring galaxy about 567 million light-years away in Pisces. Its nine rings are six more than any other known galaxy has.

Hubble's sharp imaging confirmed eight of the rings, many of them piled up near the centre, and the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii added the ninth. The two telescopes also showed which galaxy caused them. The small blue dwarf on the left plunged through the Bullseye's core about 50 million years ago, sending out rings like ripples from a pebble dropped in a pond.

Stars mostly kept to their orbits, but groups of them piled up into rings, while gas was carried outward and formed new stars. The rings appear to have spread outward almost exactly as long-standing models predicted. A thin trail of gas still links the two galaxies, now 130,000 light-years apart.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS took this image. NASA shows F475W in cyan and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: The cyan and orange are hues assigned to two filters, and the researchers say pinning down the rings bunched near the centre would have been impossible without Hubble's sharp vision.

explore: The Bullseye is about 250,000 light-years across, almost two and a half times the size of the Milky Way. The team suspects a 10th ring once existed but has faded. Hubble sees the galaxy at a slight angle, and from directly above the rings would look circular, bunched near the centre and spaced more widely farther out.
